In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles

items.title: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
items.summary: Palestinians say there was an attack by settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, while the Israeli military says the settlers fired after being attacked.
items.content:
A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.

There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.

According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.

There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.

They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.

Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Palestinian children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.

Fadda's daughter-in-law, Nema al-Fahidat, told the BBC that she died from a single bullet wound to the head. "It destroyed her brain," she said.

According to the Palestinian accounts, Fadda's son, Arafat, rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said, injuring several Palestinians, including Arafat.

"My husband, when he saw his mother, was not paying attention. He crashed into the vehicle. The vehicle was empty," Nema said.

"My husband got out of his car and tried to reach his mother and the injured young men. Then he was shot."

She added: "We tried to gather the injured people and move them away from the settler. We brought them here. But he kept firing, firing, firing. Even after we had brought the wounded young men here and moved them away from him, he continued shooting."

Nema said young Palestinians threw stones at the settlers after seeing what happened, but asked: "What can stones do against bullets?"

The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".

Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."

Later, an Israeli military source said Fadda was shot by an Israeli civilian and that there was no evidence that she had been involved in the confrontation near her home.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Israel's police force said it had opened an investigation, and that officers and forensic technicians had been collecting evidence and interviewing witnesses.

The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.

Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.

A BBC team saw settlers at the end of the street where Fadda was shot on Tuesday, as well as Israeli flags flying from four of the houses that they had moved into earlier this month.

In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.

The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.

Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.

It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".

The UK government announced on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

Israeli police arrest 10 over settler attacks on journalist and diplomats in West Bank

items.title: Trump in Asia ahead of talks with Russian and Chinese presidents
items.summary: The US president said he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Russia's Vladimir Putin "if it's available".
items.content:
US President Donald Trump has arrived in the Philippines' capital on the first leg of a trip to Asia, which will end in a meeting in China with its President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin.

A red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he walked off Air Force One in Manila. A band played one of his favourite songs, Y.M.C.A., before he was whisked away by helicopter to a hotel.

Trump's first meeting at the Asean Summit was with US partners in the Quad - India's Narendra Modi, whom he described as a "very tough man", Japan's Sanae Takaichi, who "may be even tougher", and Australia's Anthony Albanese.

"Our countries are the four corners of the free, open, stable, prosperous Indo-Pacific," the US president said.

"We have outstanding relationships and co-ordinate closely... my phone is always open," Trump added.

Many countries in South East Asia have been hit hard by Trump's tariffs and his war on Iran - but their exports to the US rose 30% last year thanks to the AI boom for which the region manufactures many of the components.

The US is hoping to draw more countries here into its "Pax Silica" tech and AI ecosystem, and away from China.

But China's huge influence in this region cannot easily be challenged, and certainly not in the few hours Trump is in the Philippines.

Later on Tuesday, Trump signed a trade deal with Thailand alongside the country's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

The US is Thailand's largest export market, accounting for 24% of its total shipments this year.

Trump then joined South East Asia leaders at a dinner, telling those gathered: "This is one of the world's most vibrant and productive regions filled with the tremendous potential."

After an overnight stay in Manila, the US president will fly to Shenzhen in China to attend a summit of Asia Pacific leaders and have nuclear talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Asked if he would also be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, Trump said: "If it's available, I would".

How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China

China is hosting the world's leaders in its AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see

items.title: Deutsche Bank nella bufera, dai file interni gli affari poco trasparenti
items.summary: Con Epstein e oligarchi russi. Sewing: 'Banca cambiata, nulla da nascondere'. In Borsa -6%
items.content:
Deutsche Bank torna nella bufera. A fare soffiare vento forte nella sede della banca a Francoforte, che è precipitata in Borsa, è un'inchiesta realizzata da oltre 230 giornalisti di 50 testate internazionali, che hanno esaminato più di 15 milioni di documenti riservati come e-mail, indagini interne, verbali del board, tutti usciti dall'istituto tedesco grazie a due whistleblower, ossia due informatori interni. Si tratterebbe di "vecchie vicende risalenti fino a 20 anni fa e la maggior parte dei problemi sarebbero stati risolti", spiega l'amministratore delegato Christian Sewing a Bild.

Da 'Inside Deutsche Bank', che ha visto in campo fra gli altri Der Spiegel, Financial Times, Le Monde e New York Times - e in Italia solo il sito investigativo IrpiMedia -, emerge un quadro a dir poco allarmante del sistema di controlli del gruppo, dove obiettivi commerciali e di profitto paiono aver prevalso sul rispetto delle norme antiriciclaggio, delle sanzioni internazionali e delle procedure interne.

Tra i capitoli più controversi c'è quello dei flussi finanziari riconducibili a Jeffrey Epstein. La banca avrebbe effettuato oltre 580 milioni di dollari di pagamenti sospetti legati al finanziere, condannato per abusi sessuali e traffico di minori e trovato infine morto nella sua cella a New York. Dalle carte emergono anche gli storici rapporti del gruppo bancario con Donald Trump. Risulta fra l'altro che nel 2017 la banca abbia inviato per errore a un commercialista documenti fiscali relativi a 1.586 conti, tra i quali quello dell'attuale presidente degli Stati Uniti.

Il ceo di Deutsche Bank, Christian Sewing, arrivato alla guida nel gruppo l'anno successivo, sarebbe stato informato dell'incidente, che non è stato comunicato ai clienti coinvolti. Dopo le presidenziali del 2016 i documenti rivelano poi che banca si è interrogata sui rischi reputazionali legati al rapporto con Trump, che le doveva 331 milioni di dollari. Successivamente, nel 2017 e nel 2019, Deutsche Bank ha individuato pagamenti sospetti che coinvolgevano le società di Trump in arrivo da Azerbaijani Laundromat nonché da un rete russa di riciclaggio legata a oligarchi vicini al Cremlino.

Nel segnalare tali operazioni alle autorità statunitense non ha però indicato che le beneficiarie erano società del presidente Usa. Sul fronte russo, inoltre, risulta che erano clienti del gruppo ben 17 funzionari e oligarchi vicini a Putin inseriti nella lista del Dipartimento del Tesoro americano già prima dell'invasione dell'Ucraina. Dopo la quale Sewing comunicava in in una mail di non volersi ritirare dal Paese. Su scala più piccola, guardando all' Italia, dove è appena scoppiato il caso Revolut, dai documenti della filiale locale di Deutsche Bank sono emerse anche qui carenze strutturali nei sistemi di controllo.

Mentre il titolo scivolava alla Borsa di Francoforte, dove ha chiuso in calo del 6%, il gruppo bancario tedesco in una nota ha sottolineato che le questioni riportate dai media risalgono anche a 20 anni fa e sono già state considerate collaborando con le autorità di vigilanza. Ha rivendicato poi che sotto la gestione di Sewing è avvenuta una trasformazione radicale e dal 2019 al 2025 sono stati fatti 7 miliardi investimenti per rafforzare i controlli e diventare così "una banca diversa", che fa utili. Deutsche Bank è "cambiata enormemente negli ultimi otto anni. Non abbiamo assolutamente nulla da nascondere", spiega Sewing il quale sottolinea come le operazioni con Jeffrey Epstein sono state un "errore della banca che non doveva verificarsi", mentre sulla Russia sono state "ridotte drasticamente le nostre attività".

Negli ultimi 25 anni il gruppo tedesco ha già sborsato 18,5 miliardi per chiudere contenziosi legati agli scandali che lo hanno travolto. Ma il capitolo non è forse ancora concluso. "Deutsche Bank ha ora la responsabilità di spiegare, con assoluta trasparenza, in che modo abbia posto rimedio alle proprie carenze e ai difetti nei controlli interni, e come intenda prevenirli efficacemente in futuro", ha dichiarato il ministro delle Finanze tedesco Lars Klingbeil.

items.title: Omicidio Bergamini, confermati 16 anni di reclusione all'ex fidanzata
items.summary: La sorella: 'Mai fatto complotti'. La difesa ha annunciato il ricorso in Cassazione
items.content:
Anche per i giudici di secondo grado Isabella Internò è colpevole. Dopo due ore di camera di consiglio la Corte d'Assise d'appello di Catanzaro ha confermato la sentenza di primo grado: 16 anni di reclusione per concorso in omicidio volontario all'ex fidanzata del calciatore del Cosenza Denis Bergamini, morto il 18 novembre 1989. Tesi rigettata dalla difesa che prepara già le contromisure annunciando battaglia anche in Cassazione.

La sera di 37 anni fa in cui morì Bergamini, originario di Argenta, Isabella era con lui. Da quel giorno un flipper giudiziario fatto di fascicoli aperti e archiviati, con ipotesi di suicidio e omicidio che si sono alternate, fino a quando la Procura di Castrovillari è arrivata all'incriminazione di Internò, condannata in primo grado dalla Corte d'Assise di Cosenza al termine di un lungo dibattimento.

Il movente del delitto, che sarebbe avvenuto tramite soffocamento, sarebbe un matrimonio mancato dopo l'aborto della Internò. Il corpo di Bergamini fu trovato riverso sull'asfalto della Ss 106 Ionica, all'altezza di Roseto Capo Spulico, nell'alto Ionio cosentino. Un tratto lungo e stretto lungo il quale si pensò che il giovane - che nel giorno della sua morte avrebbe dovuto trovarsi in ritiro con la squadra - si fosse volontariamente gettato sotto un camion.

La tesi portata a processo dall'accusa, però, sostiene che il calciatore - abbandonato il ritiro per chiarire il rapporto, ormai logoro, con Internò - sia stato soffocato e poi posizionato lungo la strada.

Nel corso del processo d'appello il pm, Luca Primicerio, aveva chiesto l'aggravio della condanna a 23 anni di reclusione, con il riconoscimento della premeditazione e che le circostanze aggravanti prevalessero sulle attenuanti generiche. Di parere diametralmente opposto la difesa. Gli avvocati Cataldo Intrieri e Angelo Pugliese non solo hanno escluso ogni coinvolgimento di Internò, ma hanno fortemente negato la tesi dell'omicidio durante l'arringa difensiva.

Internò, seduta accanto ai propri legali all'inizio dell'udienza, ha poi deciso di non tornare in aula durante la lettura della sentenza. A seguire il verdetto c'era sua sorella Catia: "Ce lo aspettavamo, adesso siamo pronti ad andare in Cassazione dove speriamo finalmente di avere giustizia", ha detto prima di andare via. Di "sentenza triste, che fa a pugni con il buon senso, con quelle che sono le risultanze del processo", ha parlato l'avvocato Intrieri, affermando che "questo processo non doveva essere celebrato a Cosenza e forse non si doveva fare nemmeno in Calabria. Adesso andiamo in Cassazione, andiamo a Roma, dove i giudici conoscono il diritto".

Scaccia ogni ipotesi di complotto la sorella di Denis Bergamini, Donata, che mai ha creduto alla tesi del suicidio del fratello: "Non ho mai fatto complotti e mai li farò perché non ne ho bisogno, perché sono una persona pulita e volevo ringraziare tutta la mia scorta umana. Mi sento anche un po' amareggiata per non essere intervenuta tante volte per come sono stati trattati coloro che hanno fatto il proprio dovere", ha detto aggrappandosi all'avvocato Fabio Anselmo che la segue da tanti anni.

items.title: Emendamento al dl sicurezza, divieto di social agli under 13
items.summary: Dai 13 ai 16 anni possibilità di gestirne uno legato a quello dei genitori
items.content:
Divieto assoluto di utilizzare i social network per i giovanissimi fino a 13 anni, divieto 'temperato' per i ragazzi tra i 13 e i 16 anni , che non potranno possedere un account autonomo ma potranno gestirne uno legato a quello dei genitori, mentre chi ha compiuto i 16 anni avrà piena libertà di aderire ad una piattaforma social: la norma, messa a punto con il contributo decisivo di Palazzo Chigi, sarà presentata nelle prossime ore da tutti i capogruppo di maggioranza come emendamento al decreto sicurezza; un emendamento che sarà aperto, si apprende, a contributi e modifiche.

Al tema però non sono mai state indifferenti nemmeno le opposizioni. Si potrà infatti adottare questo divieto perché l'Italia ha notificato il disegno di legge bipartisan Mennuni (FdI)-Madia (Iv), presentato al Senato e supportato da esponenti di maggioranza alla Commissione Europea, e questo ha consentito di negoziare con Bruxelles e avere il via libera al testo, consentendo di non dover incorrere al divieto della Commissione come accaduto con l'Austria. Tuttavia appare critica Marinanna Madia, autrice appunto del testo di legge bipartisan con la senatrice Lavinia Mennuni. "Stabilire un'età minima per accedere ai social network è una misura giusta - osserva - infatti avevamo un testo di legge pronto da mesi e già notificato a Bruxelles da molto tempo, che il governo ha di fatto osteggiato e fermato in Parlamento. Se oggi la presidente Meloni decide che invece questa misura è urgente, va bene così, sarebbe stato molto meglio non doverlo inserire in un decreto sicurezza ma, evidentemente, questo governo è capace di andare avanti solo con questi sistemi improvvisati".

Esulta il ministro dell'Istruzione, Giuseppe Valditara , che da tempo chiede una stretta, forte anche di quanto gli studi internazionali vanno attestando: il cellulare influisce in maniera negativa sull'apprendimento, causando problemi di attenzione, concentrazione, memoria e difficoltà nello studio. "Inutile dire che questo emendamento potrebbe costituire una svolta decisiva per i genitori afflitti dalla dipendenza digitale dei loro figli e per i minori verso i quali le grandi piattaforme social hanno adottato algoritmi devastanti per la loro psiche, per la salute psicofisica e per ignobili finalità commerciali", ragiona il vicepresidente della Camera, Fabio Rampelli (FdI), da sempre sensibile al tema.

Soddisfazione viene espressa da Barbara Berlusconi, da tempo impegnata con la sua fondazione in una campagna di sensibilizzazione sulle dipendenze da social. "Esprimo il mio pieno sostegno all'iniziativa legislativa, fortemente voluta dall'esecutivo, volta a regolamentare l'accesso dei minori ai social network", afferma. Un plauso arriva anche dagli psicologi di Aupi, Associazione unitaria psicologi italiani: "evidenze scientifiche - sottolineano - ci indicano quanto sia importante proteggere i bambini e gli adolescenti dai rischi connessi a un utilizzo precoce e non regolato delle piattaforme digitali".

La senatrice M5S Barbara Floridia si dice invece dispiaciuta "che si siano persi anni, durante i quali diversi Paesi in Europa e nel mondo hanno fatto passi in questo senso mentre l'Italia è rimasta incomprensibilmente ferma. Così come ci dispiace che si decida di procedere all'interno di un decreto di cui contestiamo l'impianto". La stretta italiana segue l'Eu kids Act, un nuovo pacchetto di norme comunitarie varato lo scorso settembre dalla Commissione per proteggere adolescenti e bambini dai disagi emotivi, sociali e psicologici dell'esposizione ai social media. Ma in tutto il mondo, dall'Australia, alla Francia, all'Inghilterra, i governi stanno intervenendo per limitare uso e abuso dei social da parte dei minori.

items.title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.sciencenorway.no/culture-history-history-of-science/350-years-ago-this-man-discovered-that-light-has-a-finite-speed/2737969 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50536813 Points: 234 # Comments: 72
items.content:
Ole Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light takes time to travel.

In September 1676, Ole Rømer made a prediction to the members of the Académie des Sciences in Paris.

He said that on November 9, Io, one of Jupiter's moons, would emerge from the planet's shadow ten minutes later than expected.

In doing so, he proved that light travels at a finite speed. This knowledge became crucial to how we understand the universe today.

Until then, people had believed that light travelled instantaneously from one place to another.

Ole Rømer was a Danish astronomer and physicist. In 1671, he travelled to Paris, where he spent ten years as a member of the scientific academy and an astronomer at the Paris Observatory, according to the Great Norwegian Encyclopedia .

In the years leading up to the discovery, Rømer and other astronomers had been closely observing Io, Jupiter's third-largest moon.

"Io regularly disappears behind Jupiter, and this regularity made it possible to use the moon as a clock," Jacob Wüsthoff Linder tells Science Norway.

Such a precise ‘clock’ could be useful for navigation, among other things. Ole Eggers Bjælde, a curator at the Science Museums at Aarhus University, writes this in an article on the popular-science media outlet Videnskab.dk .

Rømer studied and recorded the exact times when Io disappeared into Jupiter’s shadow and when it emerged on the other side.

Bjælde explains that because Io orbits so close to Jupiter, only one of these events could be observed on any given night.

In the days and months before Jupiter and Earth reached their closest point to each other, astronomers could observe the moon disappearing into Jupiter’s shadow.

In the period after Jupiter and Earth were closest to each other, they could see Io emerging from the shadow.

Rømer compiled detailed measurements of these events and eventually noticed a pattern.

"Rømer noticed that the eclipses occurred slightly later than expected when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and slightly earlier when Earth was moving towards Jupiter," says Linder. "He realised that this was because the light had to travel a longer or shorter distance."

In 1676, he therefore predicted that on November 9, Io would emerge from Jupiter's shadow ten minutes later than expected.

He was correct. If light travelled instantaneously, Io should have appeared ten minutes earlier.

Rømer demonstrated that light does not travel infinitely fast, says Linder. The finding was published shortly afterwards, on December 7, in Journal des sçavans .

Rømer was not the first to suggest that light has a finite speed, but he is regarded as the first to demonstrate it with evidence.

Other philosophers and scientists had previously theorised that light has a finite speed, including the Greek philosopher Empedocles, the Muslim scientists Ibn al-Haytham and Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the English philosopher and natural scientist Roger Bacon, according to Wikipedia .

"How accurate was Rømer's estimate of the speed of light compared with what we know today?"

"Not very accurate by modern standards, but impressive for 1676," says Linder.

Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Linder. That corresponds to roughly 225,000 kilometres per second, whereas the correct value is around 300,000 kilometres per second.

"So his estimate was about 25 per cent too low. What really mattered, however, was not the exact figure, but that he demonstrated that the speed of light was finite and could be measured," he says.

"It was probably a gradual process, and there were critical voices at first. The head of the observatory where Rømer worked, for example, never fully accepted his explanation. Nevertheless, his findings received support fairly quickly from prominent scientific figures such as Huygens, and later Newton," says Linder.

Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch mathematician and astronomer. He is known for developing the wave theory of light, among other things.

"The decisive blow came with James Bradley's discovery of stellar aberration about 50 years later, which provided a completely independent and strong confirmation that light has a finite speed," says Linder.

Stellar aberration is the phenomenon in which stars appear to shift slightly in the sky throughout the year because Earth moves around the Sun while light travels at a finite speed, the researcher explains.

"Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light actually takes time to travel. It was also the first time anyone had produced a reasonably realistic estimate of the speed of light," says Linder.

"Because when we look out into space, we are actually seeing things as they were when the light began its journey towards us. The farther away something is, the farther back in time we are looking," he says.

This has been important for understanding how the universe has evolved.

items.content:
We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling (https://starsling.dev), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows.

Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost.

Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762.

I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill.

We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww.

Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence

We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x)

Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills. The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself.

We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly (https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks).

We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks.

To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start. You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes.

Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge.

We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!

items.title: Carney looks to China as Trump tariffs squeeze Canada's car industry
items.summary: The PM has suggested Chinese automakers could replace American ones in Canada - but some say that would not be easy.
items.content:
Canada's car industry has become one of the clearest stress tests for Ottawa as it grapples with US tariffs on the sector.

Now Prime Minister Mark Carney has signalled that he is looking to China, where he is on a visit for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit (Apec), as part of the solution.

But that avenue is not without controversy, and is once again drawing the ire of those close to Donald Trump.

While in Cambodia earlier this week, Carney told reporters that Canada could turn to European and Asian carmakers to save its auto manufacturing sector if a trade deal with the US could not be reached.

If Canadian auto workers are "not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities.

He went on to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in China on Tuesday for their second head-to-head in less than a year. The two talked of the importance of developing their relations, and Carney said they had agreed to further tariff cuts.

Neither side mentioned vehicles specifically, though analysts suggest the issue will have been prominent in their minds.

In January, Carney said that opening the door to China's electric vehicles , external (EVs) could result in investment into Canadian-owned companies and the creation of manufacturing jobs in the sector.

American tariffs on imports of Canadian-made vehicles have led to thousands of job losses in Canada and anxiety over the future, as 90% of cars made in Canada are shipped to and sold in the US.

At the same time, China has been eyeing Canada as a potential entry-point to the North American EV market. Earlier this year, Canada announced that it would let in 49,000 EVs from China at a low tariff rate, with plans to raise that quota gradually to 70,000 by 2030.

The move was a significant break from the US, which tariffs Chinese EVs heavily to protect domestic manufacturing.

Peter Navarro, Trump's senior counsel for trade and manufacturing, warned the prime minister against cosying up to China in a post on X , external .

"Are u really threatening to play China off the US? This is offensive in the extreme," he wrote on Monday. "You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive."

His comments were reposted by Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada.

Chinese EV manufacturers like BYD and Chery have already been lobbying the Canadian government for market access.

Last week, Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu toured a Chery plant in China , external . He told reporters afterwards that Canadians could expect to see affordable Chinese EVs in Canada by early 2027.

These moves come as the toll of US tariffs on Canada's auto sector has become harder to ignore.

Stellantis, a multinational car manufacturer that made models like the Dodge Challenger in Canada, recently announced it would sell its assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario.

The facility had been idle since 2023 for a planned retooling, but what was supposed to be a temporary shutdown became permanent after Trump's tariffs.

The sale has led to speculation that a Chinese EV manufacturer could move into the facility, after Canadian media outlet CTV News reported , external , citing anonymous sources, that Stellantis was planning to lease back 25% of its plant to assemble "affordable" EVs.

The idea is unpopular with Ontario Premier Doug Ford. In a letter to Carney, he warned against opening the door for Chinese EV kits to be assembled at the Brampton plant.

China overwhelmingly builds its cars at home and ships them whole - or to be assembled in kits - overseas.

Canada's deal with China signals it is serious about shift from US

Lynette Ong, director of the China Governance Lab at the University of Toronto, said introducing Chinese auto manufacturing in Canada would be "controversial" due to fears that Canadian jobs could be lost and that the North American industry could be eroded.

"We want to make sure they're hiring Canadian workers, that they are helping train Canadian workers and that they are transferring the technology over," Ong said.

Carney noted there are "clear guardrails" in how Canada deals with China, including barring work on sensitive matters like artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

Canada has also eyed other partnerships. It is notably pursuing associate member status with the EU, and had signed a free trade deal with the Philippines earlier this week.

Just how much Canada is willing to embrace Chinese manufacturing, however, still depends on the outcome of ongoing US-Canada trade talks.

Progress has been made in negotiations, Carney recently said, but differences remain. It is unclear if Trump and Carney will speak on the sidelines of the Apec summit later this week.

items.title: Schiaffo a Putin, i missili Kiev fanno crollare il ponte della Crimea
items.summary: Zelensky esulta, l'Ue lo appoggia. Scontro Mosca-Parigi sui soldati francesi in Ucraina. Le immagini dal drone poco prima dell'impatto
items.content:
Un clamoroso schiaffo nella guerra dei ponti colpisce lo zar del Cremlino, Vladimir Putin, in vista dell'atteso trilaterale cinese con Xi Jinping e Donald Trump: gli ucraini sono infatti riusciti a distruggere il ponte di Kerch, che collega la Russia con la Crimea. Anzi collegava, perché ora il traffico è sostanzialmente interrotto dopo i missili che hanno centrato la struttura.

Mosca minimizza: "Lo ricostruiremo". Mentre Kiev esulta ma è costretta a fare i conti a sua volta con i nuovi raid russi che hanno preso di mira la capitale ucraina: il traffico sui ponti Pivnichnyi (nord) e Pivdennyi (sud) è stato nuovamente sospeso, creando immensi disagi, mentre altri raid hanno causato interruzioni al sistema idrico e di riscaldamento. Danneggiati anche alcuni tratti dei binari di superfice della metropolitana.

"La Russia colpisce quotidianamente le nostre infrastrutture, compresi i ponti, a Zaporizhia, Dnipro, Kiev e nella regione di Odessa, quella in Crimea è una operazione senza precedenti condotta in risposta a questi attacchi", ha sottolineato il presidente Volodymyr Zelensky, pubblicando la sequenza di un missile Flamingo 'made in Kiev' che colpisce il ponte Kerch. L'azienda che lo produce ha celebrato l'attacco con un emoticon stile pop corn.

I danni al ponte di Crimea, fiore all'occhiello dello zar che lo inaugurò nel 2018 attraversandolo alla guida di un camion Kamaz, sembrano molto consistenti: missili e droni hanno fatto collassare una campata di 227 metri dell'arco stradale, con i resti dell'arco di sostegno e dell'impalcato che sporgono dall'acqua sottostante. Anche la campata adiacente dell'arco ferroviario ha subito danni, ma il tratto parallelo a quello crollato sembra intatto. I detriti però sembrano ostruire del tutto il tratto navigabile sotto il ponte, che collega il Mar d'Azov al Mar Nero: il canale è largo 120 metri e profondo poco più di 8, i pezzi in acciaio sommersi potrebbero impedire il passaggio di imbarcazioni di grandi dimensioni fino a quando i detriti non saranno rimossi. Il blocco complica ancora di più l'approvvigionamento, non solo militare, della Crimea, già reso difficile da altri attacchi al ponte, nel 2022 con un camion imbottito di esplosivo l'anno successivo con i droni marini, e dalle minacce consistenti per le altre due rotte di rifornimento dalla Russia, lungo la linea del fronte orientale, e l'altra via mare.

Da Bruxelles fanno sapere che la struttura "costituisce una via di rifornimento per le truppe di Mosca e riveste un enorme valore simbolico, Kiev ha tutto il diritto di colpirlo". Al gruppo di contatto per la difesa dell'Ucraina, Zelensky ha quindi lanciato l'idea di uno scambio: "Abbiamo bisogno ora di intercettori Patriot e Iris-T dalle scorte che già avete e in cambio possiamo darvi i nuovi missili che l'Ucraina ha già ordinato, quando saranno prodotti". "Voi ci date i missili di cui abbiamo bisogno adesso e in cambio ricevete missili più nuovi e migliori", ha spiegato, chiedendo agli Stati Uniti di "non ritardare" le consegne.

Ma dalla stessa riunione nella capitale Ue è arrivato anche il monito del sottosegretario alla Difesa americano Elbridge Colby: "Mentre il dibattito pubblico si concentra sullo spettacolo degli attacchi in profondità pensati per infliggere dolore alla popolazione russa, la nostra valutazione è che non siano stati efficaci nel portare alla fine della guerra, né contribuiscano a frenare l'avanzata russa al fronte". Inoltre, con l'arrivo dell'inverno, l'Ucraina avrà bisogno di "finanziamenti solidi, questa responsabilità ricadrà però soprattutto sulle spalle dell'Europa".

Un intervento che sembra destinato a scatenare una scia di polemiche, mentre sul fronte diplomatico Parigi getta acqua sul fuoco: sostenere che i soldati francesi presenti in Ucraina partecipino direttamente al conflitto, come dichiarato dal ministro degli Esteri russo Serghei Lavrov, è "assurdo", ha detto la ministra francese con delega alle Forze armate, Alice Rufo, sottolineando che si tratta di militari impegnati esclusivamente in missioni di addestramento e manutenzione.

Parole che non hanno convinto Lavrov: "Credo che il personale militare straniero sia presente in Ucraina da più di sei mesi. E non si tratta solo di personale francese". Mosca ha "avvertito i Paesi interessati che non si tratta più di un sostegno all'Ucraina, ma di una partecipazione diretta alla guerra".

items.title: Solid 2.0
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.solidjs.com/blog/solid-2-0-the-long-hold/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50536387 Points: 218 # Comments: 56
items.content:
5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then.

A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler.

More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time.

If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design.

This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands:

This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth.

SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below.

This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability.

"But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in.

Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong.

In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix:

These handle everything from strict errors to helpful heuristics. Thanks to async in the graph we can detect waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops, poorly scaling graph shapes like wide graph fanouts and fan-ins. Today along with linting rules we can provide the best in class direction for agents at compile and at runtime.

This area is still evolving as we learn more about how agents build applications with Solid. The hard part, defining the primitives and semantics, is done. We've integrated with new dev tooling, and Chrome's Performance Tracks. And this capability goes beyond development as this observability powers things like our updated Sentry plugin so you can get the same information on your production builds.

We've also been looking at alternative syntax. Solid 2.0 adds experimental support for ReactiveScript and TSRX , both aiming to use compilation to further improve agent authoring.

I've always been a big believer that React's super power is its composability. That it allowed the ecosystem to build on its humble pieces. However, we've learned a lot since 2013. At that point composable state, async patterns, and server rendering lacked the primitives to build upon and the ecosystem came up with their own solutions. This was fine for a while but tied React's hands and fractured their ecosystem. Something only a framework as popular as React could survive.

Newer frameworks have taken more on themselves and tend to only have one metaframework, or one router. We respect React's original positioning but have updated it for 2026. It isn't about restricting the solution but giving developers the primitives to build upon in the way React originally did. Server functions are example of this. Supporting any router, and cache solution for Single-Flight Mutation is another.

We retired our metaframework SolidStart, since every primitive needed to build a Solid Metaframework is now provided by the core or by framework agnostic Vite plugins. We believe that building an opinionated layer like a metaframework shouldn't have you needing to re-implement everything again. We've taken care of the hard parts so you can focus on what you care about. And these days a lot of that work is going to be taken on by your agent. This means less to maintain but no loss in capability.

And this makes it easier for the ecosystem. Solid 2.0 only requires one Clerk or Sentry plugin since we provide the primitives for Request/Response (built on web standards) and the hooks for observability that work across any library. We've already seen success with TanStack Query and Router being as capable as anything we've built first party, bringing in Tanner's impeccable attention to detail for the APIs people love to use.

Somehow even though Solid 2.0 brings more capability to Solid, we've collapsed the surface area at almost every point. There are less primitives needed to be learnt, less ceremony around handling async. createResource , batch , startTransition , on , produce , createComputed , createMutable are all gone, because we no longer need them.

The equivalent code written for Solid 2.0 is shorter and clearer on intent. It informs our ability observe the runtime, provide better compiler errors, and removes the need for as many escape hatches (like createEffect ) that can get us in trouble. This is something we believe important in an age of AI. Safe by construction rather than by exhaustion. Reduce complexity by deriving(reducing) state rather than putting it in a reducer.

When the framework carries the guarantees, all loading state, race conditions, and cancellation logic disappears and what you are left with is the UI.

The first discussions of what a Solid 2.0 would look like started at the moment 1.0 was released. We saught feedback from the community on new reactivity ideas . The real effort started in late 2024. We announced the road to 2.0 in February 2025. Over a year of experiments followed, rewriting the reactive core from scratch until the async model held up to everything we threw at it. The beta landed in March, and the Release Candidate in August, with the API frozen.

Then 23 release candidates in 14 weeks. In that time alone, 971 pull requests were merged and 753 issues closed. We set one bar for stable. A full week with no regression in ordinary app code, and no crash or hang anywhere. It took a while to get there. By the end, the bug reports coming in were from people(agents) deliberately hunting edge cases in the deepest corners of the scheduler, and finding them.

So many people have touched the project over the past 5 years, from working on the initial reactivity prototypes, to testing the latest RC builds on their production apps. I've tried to thank as many of you as I can and attached hundreds of handles in the RC announcement. There are so many. There are also the many great organizations that have sponsored our development over the years: Sentry, Netlify, Google Chrome, JetBrains, Anomaly, Cursor, Code Rabbit, Anthropic, Tembo and so many more.

But mostly I want to thank everyone who has believed in the project. We've accomplished great things and there is much more to come. That isn't possible without all of you. Personally, the past 2 and half years have been some of the most difficult of my life, but knowing what we are building that impacts so many people leaves me with a sense of fulfillment. Solid has always been bigger than its core team, and 2.0 is the clearest proof of that yet.

The Long Hold refers to a diagnostic warning in Solid 2.0. It fires when a hold has been shown( isPending ) but sufficient time has passed since the last input. Holds were at the heart of our async work for 2.0, and we acknowledge it took a while for this all to land.

items.title: Apple down, problemi per iCloud, App Store e Apple Music: cosa sta succedendo
items.summary: Da qualche ora si stanno registrando problemi con i servizi Apple.
items.content:
Da qualche ora si stanno registrando problemi con i servizi Apple. Diversi utenti non riescono ad accedere a iCloud, altri lamentano difficoltà con l'App Store e Apple Music. Non mancano segnalazioni anche per Apple Pay. Apple ha confermato i problemi, attribuendoli a un aggiornamento interno, e ha comunicato che parte dei sistemi è già tornata operativa.

Le segnalazioni sono aumentate nel tardo pomeriggio su Downdetector, mentre la pagina ufficiale di Apple ha inizialmente continuato a indicare i servizi come disponibili. Solo successivamente sono comparsi gli avvisi relativi ai malfunzionamenti.

Su iPhone e Mac c'è chi si è ritrovato improvvisamente disconnesso da iCloud e, provando ad accedere di nuovo, ha ricevuto messaggi di errore. Non sono mancate segnalazioni di download e aggiornamenti bloccati sull'App Store, problemi con Apple Music e difficoltà nell'attivare nuovi dispositivi.

Alle 20:50 italiane, la pagina di stato di Apple indica ancora tre interruzioni e cinque servizi che hanno problemi. Le interruzioni riguardano AppleCare on Device, App Store e Volume Purchase Program. Continuano invece le anomalie relative all'accesso agli account iCloud, alle applicazioni web di iCloud, ad Apple Business, Apple School Manager e Schoolwork. Il servizio iCloud Mail, interessato dai problemi nel pomeriggio, risulta invece ripristinato.

I disservizi hanno coinvolto anche diversi strumenti dedicati agli sviluppatori, tra cui App Store Connect. Negli Stati Uniti sono stati segnalati malfunzionamenti anche nei sistemi interni degli Apple Store, con difficoltà nel completamento delle vendite. A chiarire l'origine dei problemi è stata la stessa Apple, tramite una dichiarazione condivisa dal giornalista di Bloomberg, Mark Gurman:

items.title: Phrack 73 Released
items.summary: Article URL: https://phrack.org/issues/73/introduction_md Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50535992 Points: 264 # Comments: 31
items.content:
Last year marked the 40th anniversary of Phrack so we went big. We published our anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and some additional variations at several conferences around the world including AlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon, OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challenges and had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties and had talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone.

More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of the relaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributing again. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something that made them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart.

We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners, donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working through revisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, and getting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most of that work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. We appreciate everyone who did it.

And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excited about an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realize that they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile. That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and this issue is the follow-through.

This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowing down. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eight additional articles in Line Noise. The subjects range from exploitation and reverse engineering to machine learning, hardware, and the history and culture that grew around this work.

We have container escapes through the vDSO, use-after-free exploitation, QNX userland shellcode, Linux kernel research, and a Chromium renderer sandbox escape through Skia. Elsewhere, the issue takes on Windows smart card architecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and autonomous underwater vehicles. There is also work examining backdoors in machine learning and what it means to trust an AI system. One paper takes us from PhrackCTF to two WinFSP zero-days, which is a pretty good argument for continuing to put challenges in a zine.

We also have four more articles in Phrack World History, including the story of the infamous SSH1 CRC32 vulnerability featured in The Matrix Reloaded as well as stories about blue boxing free phone calls, a confession of a hacker who tried to backdoor Linux kernel in 2003, and an early discovery of botnets for hire. Our Prophile features Halvar Flake, whose contributions to reverse engineering and security research are legendary.

In 2026, we find ourselves in a time of rapid technological change. It is hard to say what vulnerability research or red teaming will look like in another five years. AI has moved well beyond completing a line of code into agentic systems capable of analyzing source code and reverse engineering binaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities.

We can be sure that the future will require us to continue to explore new ideas, create new tools, and push the boundaries of what is possible in the face of new challenges and opportunities created by the advancement of AI and automation systems. As the effort required to put ideas into practice falls, creativity and human intuition forged through experience is valued even higher.

We hope that this release of Phrack will inspire new ideas, discussions, and collaborations that will keep the human side of hacking a critical element in shaping the future of technology and society. We will continue to do our part to support the community and provide a platform for sharing knowledge and ideas. We look forward to seeing what the future holds and we are excited to be a part of it.

Read the papers, try the ideas, and challenge the conclusions. When you find something worth sharing, write it up and send it in. We have another issue to put together, and some of you should be in it!

To those who have supported us the past three years helping to restore vitality to Phrack, we thank you.

Conferences who funded prints: Defcon, OffensiveCon, Recon, Unprompted[AU], Unprompted[US], BSides Canberra, Alligatorcon, TenguCon

Sponsors & Major Donors - WatchTowr, Elltam, Verichains, BShield, TrustedSec, Binarly, Trenchant, Praetorian (WWSUL), EFF, Blaze, EMX, Mullvad, ToorCon, Hacker Initiative, Endrazine, Dug Song, Napster, halvar, Horizon, Huku, Julio Auto, Gadi, and the rest of the people who stepped up with smaller donations.

Artists - Ian Dash, pinguino, tainted, pepper, mar, xer0, abstrakt, ToscaKaiser, h7, zir, Mick, p0rtL, netspooky, ackmage, digitalis, Tedsig42, and the many others who submitted their work for consideration.

Reviewers - barbie, bsdaemon, C, chompie, danielcuthbert, devinc, grugq, joern, jordan9001, K3, richinseattle, roddux, saber, skyper, SSHad0w, TMZ, zh4ck

All the authors past and present who are now bound to the history of phrack.

The unnamed ones who have helped us with logistics and carrying literal tons of paper around conferences to deliver them into the hands of the next generation.

All information in Phrack Magazine is, to the best of the ability of the editors and contributors, truthful and accurate. When possible, all facts are checked, all code is compiled. However, we are not omniscient (hell, we don’t even get paid). It is entirely possible something contained within this publication is incorrect in some way. If this is the case, please drop us some email so that we can correct it in a future issue.

Also, keep in mind that Phrack Magazine accepts no responsibility for the entirely stupid (or illegal) things people may do with the information contained herein. Phrack is a compendium of knowledge, wisdom, wit, and sass. We neither advocate, condone nor participate in any sort of illicit behavior. But we will sit back and watch.

Lastly, it bears mentioning that the opinions that may be expressed in the articles of Phrack Magazine are intellectual property of their authors. These opinions do not necessarily represent those of the Phrack Staff.

items.title: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
items.summary: It marks the first sanctions since the UK announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
items.content:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.

The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.

The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".

"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".

Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".

The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.

It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.

The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".

The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.

Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."

It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.

Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.

"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.

"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."

In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".

That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel , which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.

Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

items.title: MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash
items.summary: Article URL: https://microsoft.ai/news/introducing-mai-code-2-and-mai-code-2-flash/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50535885 Points: 279 # Comments: 131
items.content:
MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash : t wo new coding models built for the everyday enterprise coding tasks , delivering leading performance at a fraction of the cost of competing models.

MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance for common enterprise coding tasks and excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multi-file implementation, repo wide reasoning, and UI. It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost.

Meanwhile, MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume work such as code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost.

To deliver the best price-performance, we’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.

Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the cost. 1

MAI Code 2 is also tuned for producing great dashboards and visualizations, and excels at visual coding. In blind frontend app evaluations, reviewers preferred its results over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. 2

In addition, MAI Code 2 Flash offers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 6 5% and 20% of the cost, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks. 3

MAI Code 2 is also becoming the workhorse behind Microsoft products. From Code 2 Flash we further optimized a single model, MAI Work Flash, to serve multiple Microsoft products across M365 and Fabric IQ.

Excel: Our model is on par for accuracy and token efficiency with GPT 6 Luna across key internal Excel customer-scenario benchmarks.

PowerPoint: On key production benchmark scenarios that measure frequent PowerPoint tasks, our model performs on par with GPT 6 Luna in both quality and token efficiency.

Word: Our model performs similar to GPT 6.1 sol (while being significantly smaller) on 5 key internal benchmarks using ~42% fewer input tokens per call than GPT6.1 Sol in production.

Teams: Our model beats GPT 6 Luna at tracking decisions, filling knowledge gaps, and adapting custom instructions using up to 28% fewer tokens on instruction following and tool calling.

FabricIQ: In offline evaluation runs our MAI model outperforms GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-6-astra, and Opus-5.5 at DAX query generation, the core capability behind “Chat with your Data” for Power BI semantic models.

MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are available in GitHub Copilot, and Code 2 Flash is in limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry . Soon, we’ll be releasing it on Open Router, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo.

Learn more about customizing MAI Code 2 on our Custom Models page.

About these results Results reflect evaluations on specific coding tasks and configurations. Performance and cost comparisons vary by workload, model configuration, reasoning effort, and pricing assumptions.

items.title: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
items.summary: The Prince and Princess of Wales were joined by sporting and acting stars for the annual environmental awards ceremony.
items.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.

Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.

One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.

The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.

They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.

He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".

Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.

The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.

"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.

Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.

Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land

Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries

Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters

Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution

Fix Our Climate: Ørsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind

The Earthshot prize, first held in 2020, was inspired by former US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

Tuesday's event also saw appearances on stage from Earthshot ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor.

As well as Take That, there were also musical performances from a number of Indian artists including Shreya Ghoshal, composer and pianist Merlin D'Souza and all-female hip hop collective Wild Wild Women.

The dazzling awards night was brought to a close by musician and composer Shashwat Sachdev.

Earlier on Tuesday, William and Catherine drove in an electric rickshaw to meet the 15 finalists.

As William stepped from the vehicle, which is manufactured by prize winner Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and has a top speed of 55mph, he said: "It was quite good fun, really good fun."

The couple arrived in India on Monday for the three-day visit, which is expected to also include a meeting with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.

Their first engagement saw them play a game of street - or "gully" cricket - in Mumbai alongside Tendulkar.

items.title: Not Everything Needs an LLM
items.summary: Article URL: https://newsletter.posthog.com/p/decision-models Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50535740 Points: 90 # Comments: 37
items.content:
LLMs love to yap. Ask a simple question and you get a few hundred words of "it depends." It's annoying as hell.

This is why we love decision models like Jev for simpler tasks. You ask a structured question and get a typed answer with a probability, which looks something like this:

Choice. Which animal family do hedgehogs belong to? → Mammal, 0.99

Score. What is the current conservation status of hedgehogs? → Least Concern, 0.77

Whereas LLMs return free-form and overly confident prose, decision models make model uncertainty explicit. In a calibrated model, answers that score 0.8 are right about 80% of the time. That means a score of 0.5 is a coin flip.

We've been experimenting with them at PostHog and several use cases have made it to production. This is everything we've learned about using decision models so far: when to use them, how to use them, and mistakes to avoid.

Decision models are up to 444.6x cheaper and 193.6x faster than frontier models, 1 so you can use them to check whether you even need to make an expensive LLM call at all.

We do this in a pipeline that scrubs personal info in Replay Vision , our product that watches and summarizes user session recordings for you. Here's how it works:

Each session summary goes through 2 yes/no questions from a decision model. Using narrow questions like this cuts false flags to about a tenth of what a single question produced.

If either scores 0.4 or above, Gemini rewrites the summary without the personal info and it gets checked again.

Otherwise, it's clean and passes through the gate. In production , 98.7% skip the LLM call entirely.

Without the decision model, we'd have to keep fussing with prompts and regexes that miss things, or sending every summary to Gemini to catch the 1% that need it.

A probability score of 0.85 still means ~150 wrong answers per 1,000 checks, so plan ahead for false positives and false negatives.

In the PII example, a false positive only costs us an extra LLM call, whereas a false negative stores personal data as clean. That's why we set the threshold low at 0.4.

When false positives are the costlier mistake, use higher thresholds. For example, we recently updated the PostHog in Slack bot, so it can answer questions without being tagged . To avoid being annoying, it checks every message in a channel to see (1) whether it's asking for information, and (2) whether PostHog could answer it. Only messages that pass both at 0.85+ go through.

Takeaway: Use decision models to filter jobs before they hit an expensive LLM call, and set the threshold based on which mistake costs you more.

Our PostHog in Slack bot also uses a decision model as a model router .

When the bot gets tagged, it first checks whether the message asked for a specific model. If not, one choice question picks from the list:

“Pick the cheapest option that will most likely finish the task correctly on the first try. A failed run costs more than a smarter option.”

Each option in the list carries a short note on what that model is good for. GPT Luna is described as “a light and very cheap model. Good for short answers, lookups, summaries and very small edits.” The decision model then scores the request against each option’s text.

Different tasks, models, and providers all have different thresholds.

We were experimenting with using them to auto-merge similar logs in Error Tracking and found that thresholds changed between v1 and v2 of the same model. We had to make its thresholds configurable per PostHog project and keep the judge in shadow mode while recalibrating based on hand-labeled data .

This is one of the reasons why Fernando on our growth team pushed for a model-agnostic interface early. We now have an internal AI gateway for swapping and testing models, including self-hosted ones.

Takeaway: Use a choice question to route free-form LLM requests to the cheapest model that can handle it. Keep in mind that thresholds don't carry over, so set them per task and per model.

If a question requires more context or chains of reasoning, it's better to use an LLM. However, you can still use a decision model if you have a way to flatten, or pre-process the input, so it's checkable at face-value.

In Replay Vision, when a user searches for a theme like "onboarding friction," there's a chance for the query to return a few unexpected results because of the way embedding distance works.

A decision model can’t "Rank the top 10 sessions that contain summaries that match the user's search query." It’s too complicated.

Instead, we use the embeddings first to derive an initial list of session recordings to pass to the decision model. Then, the only task left for the decision model is to look at how closely each result in the list matches the user's original search term:

"Does this summary describe a session that matches what the search looks for?"

Results are then reranked by that probability. On 20 test queries, this improved ranking quality by about 25%.

We've tried using a decision model for multi-step reasoning before. Before embeddings were ready in Replay Vision, we tried ranking a "Highlights" feed of sessions worth a human's time. The questions were:

If so, why is it worth watching? (With choices like “error on screen,” “slow or stuck,” “user confused”, “user gave up", etc.)

Processing these two questions in order required an hourly job that sent large requests – up to 32 sessions and 12-38k tokens each – which flooded the model server and blocked other products' calls for hours.

So yes, technically, you can chain decision models into multi-step judgments, but it's not operationally worth it. Leave that to LLMs, or do the heavy lifting before the decision model sees the data like in the embedding search example above.

Takeaway: Decision models judge what's in front of them in a single pass. Leave multi-step reasoning to LLMs.

Decision models can take any job where an LLM is overkill, either because it's too slow or too expensive.

One example is our smarter chart picker for SQL queries. PostHog used to pick a visualization using deterministic rules like:

A date column, a number column and multiple rows → Line chart

Now, a decision model looks at both the SQL itself if your org opts in, and the first three rows of the results to suggest a better chart.

The example below is based on a simple query about pageviews by browser. The original rules picked a basic aggregate line chart; with Jev, it chose a bar chart split by browser:

Still, out of curiosity, we tried Jev on ranking our internal PR review agent's findings with five noul questions that roughly asked if the change is worth a developer's attention. The results were inconclusive with an AUC of 0.52.

If Jev were an LLM, we’d solve this by sending more context, but Jev can’t handle large requests. Its long-context mode is also slower and less accurate. 2 Typical decision models just aren’t built for this kind of reasoning.

Hybrid decision models like Jeeves can help bridge this gap, though. Developed by our in-house AI research team , Jeeves is a decision model that reasons before deciding when it’s unsure.

It's now our default for any decision call at PostHog that doesn't name a model, and there are similar variations by other developers, like Kev .

Takeaway: Use decision models as evaluators for inputs that are too simple for a language model, yet too fuzzy for a regex. Anything more complex is still too much to hand over to a decision model. For now, at least.

Words by Jina Yoon, who expects this article to be obsolete in two months.

Why we’re moving our warehouse product off DuckDB – Benjamin Knofe-Vider

The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning – Ali Behrouz, Vahab Mirrokni

We made experiment queries 4x faster using precomputation – Juraj Majerik

Product Manager, Observability (ex-founder or ex-product engineer)

Jev takes 64k tokens per request and 32k per question by default. And even though TypeSafe added an opt-in header that raises both to 262k, they still warn that the long-context mode is slower and less accurate. Source: TypeSafe Docs
